Engine images: the submitted fixture frame strips (preview scenes, labelled FIXTURE) and this film's native-4K captures of the unmodified project with scripted input (one with a film camera added by the capture script; pause and hide set from code; all labelled). Difference images are computed analysis and labelled. No game change, no commit, no push, no publication.

beats.narration_text: Hola, this is Liam, narrating for Jonathan. The prompt on screen is a reconstruction for this film, not a saved session. It asks Walker to give a subway extraction shooter its first particle effects: dust when the player lands, and dust in the air that lives only while the lights are on. At source revision one, eight, two, eight, b, b, six, b, the answer is two effects, four tests, a cost script, and eighteen fixture strips.

beats.narration_text: The game: a survivor in a subway base. Effect A is landing dust. Its job is to say you touched the ground, and its event is a new signal, landed, on the character's body. Effect B is dust hanging in the air, for atmosphere. Its condition is the ceiling lights: on, the dust is there; off, it is gone.

beats.narration_text: Before anything was built, I wrote the intent. Timing: strongest at a tenth and a half of a second, gone at one point six. Scale: about one and a half capsules wide. Two layers: dust, and a faint ring on the floor. And the retrigger rule: a second landing restarts it, so at most one burst is alive.

Line one seventeen, twenty-four particles; one-shot, all at once on line one twenty-one. Process: what each particle does over its life, here a ParticleProcessMaterial on line one twenty-four. Draw: what each particle looks like, a quad mesh on line one twenty-five.

beats.narration_text: That wish broke the brief's ankle-height rule, so I revised the intent first, then tuned. Revision r one changed one setting: the dust quad from eight to thirty-two centimetres. The agent edited before my approval, and sent its prediction afterwards; I approved after the fact and kept it. Its prediction held at most frames, including thirty: bigger, still visible at point seven seconds. At frame fifty it missed. I stopped tuning here, on my in-game judgement.

beats.narration_text: Now the event. After every move, the body asks: am I on the floor now, and was I in the air last frame? Then this frame is a landing, and line one thirteen emits landed, once. Line one fifteen is a fix: on load, the physics engine pushed the player up out of the floor, which counted as a landing. The test caught it.

props.title: The event · humanoid.gd
props.code:
func _notify_landing() -> void:
	var on_floor := is_on_floor()  # First we read where the move just left us: on the floor or in the air
	# If we have stood on the floor before, are on it now, and were in the air last frame, we have come back to the floor: this frame is the landing
	if _has_touched_floor and on_floor and not _was_on_floor:
		landed.emit()  # So we announce it once; the landing dust hears it and plays at the feet
	_was_on_floor = on_floor  # Then we remember this frame's state, so next frame standing still does not count as landing again
	_has_touched_floor = _has_touched_floor or on_floor  # And once we have stood on the floor, later landings count; the first touch on load does not
props.inspectorLabel: Source notes — derived from these lines
output: Written by the agent (prompt-3), fix chosen by me

beats.narration_text: In the running game, with scripted key presses. Two single jumps: dust and a ring at the feet. Then four rapid jumps, mostly while moving left, each landing inside the last burst's lifetime. Each time, the old dust is cleared and plays again where the feet are. Replayed at twice the size: no pile-up.
beats.role_note: Real native-4K engine footage. Scripted Space/A input (captures/landing-run-02); second half is the same frames as a labelled 2x crop. Labels burned in by scripts/prepare_media.py. No retiming; a labelled final-frame hold only if narration is longer.

qc.contrast_reason: Edge-to-edge native Godot render; the essential text is the label strip.

beats.narration_text: The trigger listens to landed. It moves to the feet, then calls restart on both emitters, not emitting equals true. Restart clears a burst that is still alive and starts a new one here. Setting emitting would do nothing to a live one-shot burst.

props.title: The retrigger · landing_dust_trigger.gd
props.code:
func _on_body_landed() -> void:
	global_position = body.global_position  # First we stand on the landing point (the body's origin is at its feet); with local_coords off, the new burst is born here
	_dust.restart()  # Then we clear what is left of the old dust and start a new cloud
	_ground_ring.restart()  # And the same for the ring on the floor, so both layers start on the same frame
props.inspectorLabel: Source notes — derived from these lines

notes.label: Rule
notes.value: restart(): at most one burst alive

beats.narration_text: The retrigger strip: a second landing on frame twenty-five, half a metre away. On twenty-five the old dust is gone; on twenty-seven the new ring starts at the new spot; the old cloud never comes back. The state test checks the same rule by real key presses: with emitting equals true instead, it fails.

beats.narration_text: Effect B has a different job: atmosphere, not feedback. Its first intent was a small box of dust under one light. It must already be settled on its first frame, frozen when paused, gone when hidden or when the lights go off. Later I revised it to fill the whole room, lit by the lights.

props.title: Effect B · the intent block
props.status: CHANGE-BRIEF.md, Effect B and its 2026-11-12 revision
props.source: walker-survival-shooting @ 1828bb6b (course repository, assignment-6) · CHANGE-BRIEF.md, Effect B

beats.narration_text: Its process material uses what Effect A does not. A box emission shape, moved to the room's centre by an offset. Turbulence, so specks drift on noise instead of straight lines. And an opacity ramp with several peaks, so each speck twinkles in and out. The draw material adds light rather than covering, and preprocess runs six seconds before the first frame.

First strip, r zero: a hundred and fifty specks under one light. I said the size should vary, and it was too dense. Revision r one changed one setting, amount, from a hundred and fifty to ninety. The agent proposed first this time; its prediction, about seventy changed pixels, measured seventy-four. Kept.

beats.narration_text: Then, in the game, I had to walk up to a light to see anything. So I asked for the whole room, lit by the lights, sizes from three millimetres to three centimetres, all at once. That is a redesign recorded in the brief, not a tuning round. Three thousand specks was too dense and too bright; I chose nine hundred at half brightness, then thirteen hundred.

beats.narration_text: The condition lives in a listener on the dust. Lights on: show it and restart once, which reruns preprocess. Lights off: hidden that frame, and no new births. It never touches the lights; it only reads them.

props.title: The condition · light_dust_listener.gd
props.code:
func _on_lights_changed(lights_on: bool) -> void:
	if lights_on:  # If the lights are on, the dust under them shows
		if visible:  # If we are already shown (scene load), showing again would not fire visibility_changed, so we restart here ourselves
			_restart()
		else:  # Otherwise we only show; visibility_changed then calls _on_visibility_changed(), which restarts once, so restart() does not run twice
			visible = true
	else:  # Otherwise the dust goes away with the light
		visible = false  # Hidden from this frame on; visibility_changed also stops births
		emitting = false  # And we stop births here too, in case we were already hidden and no visibility_changed came
props.inspectorLabel: Source notes — derived from these lines
output: Written by the agent (prompt-5-wire), changes asked by Claude

beats.narration_text: In the game, through a film camera near the first light, with scripted F presses at the switch. The inset is computed: it shows where the dust is. Lights off, the dust is gone that frame. Lights on, it is back already spread out. Paused from code, it freezes. Hidden, gone; shown again, full at once.

Line two sixty-one is my brief's box: a random point in a cube, times emission box extents, seven, one point three, four point five. Line two sixty-three adds the offset, zero, point one five, three point two. That is why the box is fourteen by nine metres and centred on the room.

beats.narration_text: Line two fifty-three runs every frame: the colour is multiplied by the colour ramp at the particle's age. That is my opacity ramp, zero, point six, point one five, point nine, and so on, so each speck brightens and dims several times. Gravity is lines three ninety-seven and four ten, but both effects set gravity to zero.

beats.narration_text: The tests read settings back from the loaded scene. First they ask ClassDB whether each property name exists in this engine, so a stale name fails loudly. Then every value is compared with the brief.

props.title: Read-back · test_landing_dust_config.gd
props.code:
func _check_property_names() -> void:
	for cls_name in PROPERTY_NAMES:  # We go through the classes one by one
		var known := {}  # The names this engine really has on this class, including inherited ones; filled just below
		for prop in ClassDB.class_get_property_list(cls_name):  # ClassDB gives us every property of the class and its parents
			known[prop.name] = true  # We remember each name so the lookup below is a plain dictionary check
		for prop_name in PROPERTY_NAMES[cls_name]:  # Then for every name we read on this class
			_check("ClassDB: %s.%s exists" % [cls_name, prop_name], known.has(prop_name))  # If the engine does not have it, this line says which one
props.inspectorLabel: Source notes — derived from these lines

beats.narration_text: All four pass, headless at sixty frames per second: a hundred fifty-seven, twenty-seven, a hundred ten and forty-one. The state tests press real keys: Space and D for landings, S and F for the lights, and check restart counts, pause and hide.

Then I broke it. Mutation one: the Godot three name, initial velocity. The engine loaded it silently; in four point seven that name is an editor-only pair, so the float is dropped and the minimum speed becomes zero. Only the read-back caught it. Mutation two: amount thirty, brief unchanged. Both exit one.

The headless price, the chapter's way: time each frame as the gap between two process frames, three hundred frames, three repeats, round-robin, with an empty-scene control and a ten thousand CPU-particle control.

props.title: Headless CPU price · cost_effects.gd
props.code:
var start := Time.get_ticks_usec()  # Then we time each frame on its own: the gap between two process_frame signals
	var total := 0
	for i in TIMED_FRAMES:
		_tick_landing(name, base, landings)
		await process_frame
		var now := Time.get_ticks_usec()
		times.append(now - start)  # One frame's wall time in microseconds; the spread below comes from these
		total += now - start
		start = now
	(_means[name] as Array).append(total / 1000.0 / TIMED_FRAMES)  # This repeat's mean, ms per frame
props.inspectorLabel: Source notes — derived from these lines

notes.label: Cases
notes.value: empty · off · A · B · CPU control

beats.narration_text: Empty scene: point zero zero four milliseconds. Ten thousand CPU particles: one point eight eight. So the script sees CPU work. Effect A adds point zero zero six, Effect B point zero two five, both inside the noise. That is expected: headless Godot uses a dummy renderer, so GPU simulation and drawing never run. Near zero says nothing about the GPU.

props.title: Result · headless price near zero
props.status: Recorded output of cost_effects.gd, copied verbatim

beats.narration_text: The GPU price, on an R T X fifty-seventy Ti laptop GPU, windowed, vsync off, lights kept on, reading the engine's measured GPU time. Effect B adds point zero one seven milliseconds against a point three budget; Effect A about point zero zero one against point two. With vsync on, F P S reads one forty-four; my debug key V turns it off, and F P S rises to about thirteen fifty, so the comparison is not capped.

beats.narration_text: What no headless run can show: whether anything is visible, reads well, or is too bright. That is the strips and my own play. One thing I am not sure of: Effect A's visibility box. Since r one, the puffs reach point two three metres up and point six eight out, beyond the box's point two and point six, so they may vanish early at the screen edge. Enlarging it is my next step.

props.title: Limits and what remains uncertain
props.status: TEST-REPORT Use It · README Known limitations

beats.narration_text: Agent mistakes I caught: it forgot the fixed seed on the preview; its first wiring fired the dust on scene load; and in tuning it edited before I approved. Claude's strip readings I overruled: it said the dust was too warm, cut flat by the floor, hidden by the capsule, and not six to eight separate puffs. In the game I do not see those as problems. A human lands, not a mech.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Built: two effects, their triggers, four tests, a cost script and a GPU helper. Human: the brief, every verdict, the redesign values, the shader conversion and the play test. AI: the scenes, tests, previews and strip readings, by Claude Code with Opus five point five; and this narration, by local Kokoro. Textures: none from outside; both effects draw with gradient textures defined in their scene files. Shown: revision one, eight, two, eight, b, b, six, b. Next: enlarge Effect A's visibility box.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Please use Walker on my Godot project. Read my change brief and my landing dust scene. Enlarge the Dust emitter's visibility box so it contains the r1 puffs. Before you change anything, predict what my edge-of-screen check will show, then capture again and compare. The prediction is the point: write down what should change before you look. This was Liam, narrating for Jonathan.
